spec: Wire the hangar door controller's 'moving' signal to Arduino pin 2 (a steady 5V HIGH while the door is in motion, 0V when stopped) and an active buzzer from pin 8 to ground. The sketch uses only the Arduino core and a 10 ms loop delay.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: Three normally-open switches (two coin slots and a service button) connect pins 2, 3 and 4 to ground, using the internal pull-ups, and the onboard LED on pin 13 is the status light. Each press on a coin slot adds one credit and prints the running total over serial at 9600 baud; pressing the service button resets credits to zero. Inputs are debounced with a 25 ms lockout, and the LED blinks at 500 ms on / 500 ms off regardless of credits. The sketch only uses the Arduino core and prints a startup message on boot.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: Buttons on D2 (up) and D3 (down) and normally-closed limit switches on D4 (top) and D5 (bottom) all connect to GND with internal pull-ups, so a pressed button or an open/broken switch wire reads LOW. The H-bridge inputs are D9 (up) and D10 (down), and the onboard LED on D13 lights whenever the motor is energised. Holding up drives the chair up unless the top switch is open, holding down drives it down unless the bottom switch is open, and releasing both buttons stops the motor immediately. If the direction is reversed the sketch stops the motor and waits at least 120 ms before energising the opposite input, and pressing both buttons at once always stops the motor.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: An HX711 load-cell amplifier is wired with its DT data pin to Arduino D2 and SCK clock to D3; the onboard LED is on D13 and serial runs at 9600 baud. The sketch bit-bangs 24-bit HX711 readings, converts them to kilograms using a fixed calibration of 2280 counts per kg and a stored tare, and prints a timestamped weight line whenever the reading changes by more than 0.02 kg. Every 60 seconds it prints a LOG line with the current weight and rewrites the tare to EEPROM address 0, and it toggles the LED every 500 ms. On boot it loads the tare from EEPROM, falling back to 8420000 if the stored value is 0 or -1.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A TMP36 temperature sensor output feeds Arduino A0, a 5V relay module controlling the chiller compressor is driven from D7, and the onboard LED on D13 mirrors the relay state. The sketch samples temperature every 2 seconds and turns cooling on when the reading exceeds 18.5 C, turning it off when it drops below 17.5 C. To protect the compressor, the relay must stay on at least 60 seconds and stay off at least 120 seconds between changes. If the sensor reads below 2 C or above 30 C, cooling is forced off and the reading is printed over serial at 9600 baud.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: The solenoid striker is wired to digital pin 9 through a logic-level MOSFET gate, with a 10k pulldown on the gate; a momentary button to ground sits on pin 2 using the internal pullup, and the onboard LED on pin 13 lights during activity. On power-up the sketch waits one hour (3,600,000 ms) and then strikes the current hour count, starting at 1 and cycling 1 through 12, with each strike energizing pin 9 for 120 ms and 400 ms between strikes. Pressing the button triggers a single immediate strike. The sketch uses delay() inside strikeOnce(), so button presses during a strike are ignored until it finishes.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: An LM35 temperature sensor output feeds A0 (5V reference, 10mV per degree C), a piezo buzzer sits on D9, the onboard LED is on D13, and a momentary mute button connects D2 to ground with the internal pull-up enabled. The fridge must stay between 2.0 and 6.0 degrees C; if the reading stays outside that band for 60 seconds continuously, the buzzer sounds and D13 blinks every 250ms. Pressing the button silences the buzzer while the LED stays lit, and the alarm clears only when the temperature returns inside 2.4 to 5.6 degrees C (0.4 degree hysteresis). The sketch prints temperature and alarm state over serial at 9600 baud every half second.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A float switch is wired from Arduino pin 2 to ground (internal pull-up enabled), a manual override pushbutton from pin 4 to ground, and the pump relay coil is driven from pin 9 through a transistor with pin 13 lighting an indicator LED. When the float switch closes (pin 2 reads LOW) or the manual button is pressed, the pump turns on and runs for at most 8 seconds, then shuts off. After any stop the pump will not restart for 30 seconds unless the float is still closed, and switch changes must be stable for 50 ms before they are accepted.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: Wiring: a push button from D2 to GND (internal pull-up), a hobby servo signal on D9 with 5V and GND, a relay/solenoid driver input on D7, and the onboard LED on D13. Pressing the button once runs a blocking reset cycle: the servo sweeps from 0 to 90 degrees over 1200 ms, holds 300 ms, sweeps back to 0 over 1200 ms, then the solenoid fires HIGH for 400 ms. The D13 LED blinks at 250 ms intervals during the cycle and stays solid when idle; the button is debounced for 50 ms and waits for release so one press equals one cycle.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A momentary pushbutton connects D2 to ground (internal pull-up enabled), a hobby servo signal wire goes to D9, an active buzzer is on D8, and the onboard LED is D13. Pressing the button toggles the guard: opening drives the servo to 90 degrees, lights D13, and gives an 80 ms beep; closing returns it to 0 degrees, clears the LED, and gives a 40 ms beep. If the guard stays open for more than 4000 ms it closes itself automatically, and button presses are debounced with a 25 ms window.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: An Arduino Uno drives a model canal lock. Three pushbuttons wired from pins 2, 3 and 4 to ground use the internal pull-ups, so a press reads LOW. Pin 9 feeds a PWM motor driver for the single working gate (value 180 when open, 0 when closed) and pin 10 drives the water pump at full PWM (255) when toggled on. Pressing the pin 2 button opens the gate, pin 3 closes it, and pin 4 toggles the pump on and off, with each press debounced by a 300 ms delay and logged over Serial at 9600 baud. The second gate is deliberately ignored because it is glued shut on this model.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: Wire a 10k NTC thermistor from 5V to A0, with a 10k resistor from A0 to GND, and connect an active-low relay module input to D7 (relay COM/NO switch the heater). The sketch reads the thermistor every 50 ms, converts it to Celsius with the beta equation (beta 3950, 10k nominal at 25 C), and turns the heater on when temperature falls below 63 C and off when it rises above 67 C. It prints the measured temperature and heater state over serial at 9600 baud once per second.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A 10k potentiometer is wired as a voltage divider with its ends to 5V and GND and its wiper to analog pin A0; a standard hobby servo's signal wire goes to digital pin 9, power to 5V, and ground to GND. The sketch reads the pot every 20 ms and maps the 0-1023 reading linearly to a servo angle of 45-135 degrees, so a mid-scale reading near 512 commands about 90 degrees (straight rudder). The servo only updates when the newly mapped angle differs from the last commanded angle by more than 8 degrees, which suppresses jitter around center. Each loop also prints the raw pot value and computed angle over Serial at 9600 baud.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A 4-digit common-cathode display is multiplexed on pins 4-7 and 10-13 for segments A-G/DP, with digit commons on A0-A3 (LOW lights a digit). A START button on pin 2 and a STOP button on pin 3 use internal pull-ups and are active LOW; the solenoid relay is on pin 8 (HIGH opens the valve) and a buzzer is on pin 9. Pressing START loads 300 seconds, opens the valve, and counts down once per second, showing MM:SS; the valve closes and the display reads 0000 when the countdown reaches zero or STOP is pressed. During the final 10 seconds the buzzer toggles every 500 ms.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: An HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor is mounted above the tank: its trigger is on D2 and echo on D3, with the onboard LED on D13. Every 500 ms the sketch fires a 10 us trigger pulse, measures the echo width (timeout 30 ms), and converts it to distance in cm using 0.0343 cm/us divided by 2. It assumes the sensor sits 5 cm above a 60 cm tank whose empty water surface reads 55 cm, computes water level as 55 minus (distance minus 5), clamps it to 0-60 cm, and prints distance, level and rounded percent over 9600 baud serial. The LED turns on when the tank is below 15 percent, and a failed echo prints 'err'.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A hall-effect or reed sensor on D2 (INPUT_PULLUP, active LOW) pulses once per carousel revolution; a motor driver PWM input is on D9 and a status LED on D13. The sketch measures the microsecond interval between falling edges and targets a 2,000,000 us period (30 rpm) using a proportional governor with KP = 0.00008 PWM counts per microsecond of error, starting at PWM 120 and clamped to 0-255. If no pulse arrives for 5 seconds it drives PWM to 255 to kick the motor and lights the LED, clearing the LED on the next valid period. The first pulse is ignored because there is no prior timestamp.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A DHT22 humidity sensor sits on digital pin 2 (with its data line pulled up to 5V), a relay module driving the ultrasonic mist maker is on pin 7, and the onboard LED on pin 13 mirrors the relay. The sketch reads humidity every 2.5 seconds and turns the mist maker on when relative humidity drops below 80%, then off once it climbs above 88%. A minimum 20-second on-time and 60-second off-time prevent short cycling, and a hard 5-minute maximum run cuts the relay regardless. Humidity readings are printed to Serial at 9600 baud.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: A 5V relay module's IN pin connects to Arduino D7, and its VCC/GND go to the Uno's 5V and GND; the relay is active-LOW, so D7 LOW energizes the pump and D7 HIGH keeps it off. Two momentary pushbuttons connect D2 (start) and D3 (stop) to GND, using the internal pullups so idle reads HIGH and pressed reads LOW. Pressing start turns the pump on for exactly 90000 ms (90 s), then the sketch turns it off automatically; pressing stop at any time turns it off immediately. The sketch uses millis() for timing so the stop button stays responsive during a run, and it debounces each button with a 30 ms delay plus a wait-for-release loop.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: Wire a momentary pushbutton between pin 2 and ground (internal pull-up is used, so no external resistor), a motor driver signal input to pin 9, a piezo buzzer to pin 8, and the onboard LED on pin 13. Pressing the button starts the drum motor and lights the LED for exactly 480000 ms (8 minutes), ignoring the button while a roast is running. When the time expires the motor and LED turn off and the buzzer beeps three times (200 ms on, 200 ms off). Serial output at 9600 baud reports start and done events.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A pushbutton connects between digital pin 2 and ground (internal pull-up enabled), a 10k potentiometer wiper goes to A0 with its ends to 5V and GND, and the safelight control signal drives digital pin 9. Pressing the button starts a timed interval whose length is set by the pot, mapped from 5000 ms at pot minimum to 120000 ms at pot maximum, and pin 9 goes HIGH for that duration then LOW. The sketch prints the chosen time and a done message over serial at 9600 baud, and ignores button presses while a timing cycle is active.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A momentary push button connects pin 2 to ground (internal pull-up enabled), a relay or MOSFET driving the lamp is on pin 9, and the onboard LED on pin 13 mirrors the lamp state. Pressing the button when the lamp is off turns it on and starts a 120000 ms (2 minute) timer; pressing it again while on restarts that timer from zero. When the 2 minute period elapses the lamp and status LED turn off automatically. Button contacts are debounced with a 30 ms window so a single press is not counted twice.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A passive buzzer sits on pin 9 (through a transistor), a momentary pushbutton to ground on pin 2 with the internal pull-up enabled, and the onboard LED on pin 13. A short press does nothing; holding the button for more than 4000 ms triggers a three-beep alarm pattern of 180 ms on and 120 ms off per beep, with the LED lit for the whole pattern. Button edges are debounced with a 25 ms window, and press/release/alarm/done events are printed at 9600 baud.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: Wire a 4x4 matrix keypad with rows on Arduino pins 2-5 and columns on pins 6-9 (columns use internal pull-ups). Connect a solenoid lock to pin 10 (HIGH energizes/unlocks), a green LED to pin 11, and a red LED to pin 12 through 220-ohm resistors. The player types the 4-digit code 1234 and presses '#' to submit; '*' clears the entry. On a correct code the lock stays energized and the green LED lights for 5 seconds, then both turn off; on a wrong code the red LED blinks on for 1 second and the entry is cleared.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A 100k NTC thermistor (B=3950) is wired from A0 to GND with a 10k resistor from A0 to 5V, and a solid-state relay control line goes to D9 with the onboard LED on D13. The sketch reads the NTC every 500 ms, converts resistance to Celsius via the beta equation, and turns the SSR on when temperature falls below 91.5 C and off when it rises above 94.5 C, targeting a 93 C setpoint. Each cycle it prints the temperature to serial at 9600 baud followed by HEAT or IDLE.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: Wire a momentary push button from D2 to GND (internal pull-up enabled), an analog flame sensor output to A0, and an active-HIGH igniter relay to D8; the onboard LED on D13 mirrors the relay. The relay energizes only while the button is held and the A0 reading is at or below 400 counts, and it cuts off immediately if A0 rises above 400 or the button is released. A hard 8000 ms timeout turns the relay off even if the button stays pressed, and button edges are debounced for 30 ms. Serial output at 9600 baud logs each igniter ON/OFF transition.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A float switch on D2 (INPUT_PULLUP, reads LOW when water is present) triggers the gate, and a limit switch on D3 (INPUT_PULLUP, LOW when the gate is fully open) stops the opening motor. The motor relay is on D8 and is active LOW, so the gate opens when D8 goes LOW; the onboard LED on D13 is HIGH only while the gate is held open. When water is detected the gate opens until the limit switch trips or 20 seconds pass, stays open for a 15-second pass window, then closes for up to 20 seconds before returning to idle. The float switch is debounced with a 50 ms window so splashes do not chatter the gate.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: A 10k potentiometer is wired as a voltage divider with its outer legs to 5V and GND and its wiper to A0; a blower motor is driven through a transistor whose base/gate connects to digital pin 9 (a PWM pin), with the motor's own supply sharing ground with the Uno. The sketch reads the knob (0-1023), maps it to a PWM value (0-255), forces the output to 0 whenever the mapped value is below 20 so the motor doesn't buzz at low settings, and smooths changes by moving a quarter of the way toward the new value each 50 ms loop. It also prints the raw knob reading and the smoothed motor value to Serial at 9600 baud for debugging. Turning the knob fully clockwise should give full speed (255) and fully counterclockwise should stop the motor.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A K-type thermocouple amp output feeds A0 (10mV per degree C, 0.5V offset), a MOSFET gate on D9 drives the kiln element, a pushbutton to GND is on D7 with internal pullup, and a 16x2 LCD is wired in 4-bit mode to D12,D11,D5,D4,D3,D2. The sketch ramps the setpoint from ambient at 2.5 C per minute until it reaches 516 C, then holds that setpoint for 30 minutes before latching off and blinking the D13 LED. Heating turns on when measured temperature is more than 1 C below setpoint and off when more than 1 C above. Pressing the button restarts the ramp from the current temperature.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: PTT switch connects D2 to ground when pressed (internal pull-up enabled); D7 drives the radio KEY line (HIGH = unkeyed, LOW = transmit); D13 drives a status LED through the board's built-in resistor. When PTT is held, the sketch keys the radio and lights the LED; after 180000 ms (3 minutes) of continuous transmit it unkeys the radio and blinks D13 every 250 ms until PTT is released. Releasing PTT at any time unkeys the radio, turns the LED off, and resets the timer for the next transmission.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: An Arduino Uno drives a brushless lift fan ESC from pin 9 using Servo-style pulses of 1000 us (idle) to 2000 us (full lift). A momentary pushbutton from pin 2 to ground toggles the fan on and off with 30 ms software debounce, and a 10k potentiometer on A0 sets the lift level from 0 to 100 percent. On power-up the sketch holds the ESC at 1000 us for 3 seconds to arm it, then mirrors the fan state on the pin 13 LED. The trim pot is sampled every 50 ms and mapped linearly from the 0-1023 ADC range to 0-100 percent.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A pH probe module feeds analog input A0; its output is 2.5 V at pH 7.0 and changes 0.18 V per pH unit. A peristaltic pump relay is wired to digital pin 7 and is active HIGH. The sketch samples A0 eight times, converts the average to pH, and if pH is above 5.90 it runs the pump for 1500 ms, waits 10 seconds, and repeats until pH is back within 0.10 of the 5.80 target. Total pump-on time per correction cycle is capped at 8000 ms, and pH plus dosing decisions are printed to Serial at 9600 baud.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: An Arduino Uno drives a relay H-bridge on D7 (raise) and D8 (lower) for the conditioner gate motor. Limit switches on D4 (up) and D5 (down) and an E-stop on D6 are normally-closed to ground with internal pullups, so an open wire reads as triggered; a START button on D2 and a PASS button on D3 are momentary to ground. Pressing START lowers the gate until the down limit or a 6-second timeout, then waits for PASS to be held; releasing PASS raises the gate until the up limit or another 6-second timeout. Opening the E-stop immediately cuts both relays and blinks the D13 LED at 2 Hz until the E-stop is restored and the gate is at the up limit.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A thermocouple amplifier output feeds Arduino A0 and a relay module control input is on pin 7, wired active LOW so the kiln element runs when pin 7 is LOW. The sketch reads A0 eight times, averages, and converts at 10 mV per degree C with 5 V over 1023 counts, so 1200 C corresponds to about 4.9 V on A0. When the computed temperature reaches 1200 C the relay is driven HIGH to cut the element, and it is only re-enabled once the reading falls back to 1100 C or below. Status lines with the temperature and relay state are printed to Serial at 9600 baud every 500 ms.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: A slotted optical sensor with an open-collector output is wired to Arduino Uno pin 2 (with the internal pull-up enabled) and GND, and the Uno reports over USB serial at 9600 baud. Each falling edge on pin 2 marks one spindle slot passing; pulses closer than 2000 microseconds apart are treated as bounce and ignored. The sketch computes RPM as 60,000,000 divided by (microseconds between pulses times the number of slots per revolution, set to 1), and prints 'RPM: <value to 1 decimal>   pulses: <count>' about every 200 ms. With one slot, a 1000 RPM spindle produces a 60,000 microsecond period and should read 1000.0 RPM.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: An Arduino Uno has a start push button from pin 2 to ground (internal pull-up used), a heater relay signal on pin 8, a drum motor relay signal on pin 9, and the built-in LED on pin 13. Relays are active HIGH. Pressing the button starts a 30-minute (1,800,000 ms) cycle: the motor relay turns on, then 500 ms later the heater relay and LED turn on. When millis() shows 1,800,000 ms have elapsed, the heater turns off, 200 ms later the motor and LED turn off, and the dryer waits for another button press.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: Relay modules for the main and spare lamps are driven from Arduino pins 7 and 8 (active-low), an LDR divider on A0 senses whether the lamp is lit, and a pushbutton to ground on pin 2 forces a manual swap. Every 2 seconds the sketch reads A0; if the reading falls below 300 it assumes the lamp has failed and toggles to the other relay, waiting 200 ms between turning one off and the other on. Pressing the button performs the same swap immediately, and all events are logged over serial at 9600 baud.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: A servo's signal wire goes to Arduino pin 9, its power to 5V and ground to GND. A pushbutton connects pin 2 to ground, using the internal pull-up so the pin reads LOW when pressed. On power-up the servo moves to 20 degrees and stays there; when the button is pressed the servo swings to 110 degrees, holds for 1500 ms, then returns to 20 degrees, ignoring further presses until the hold finishes. The onboard LED on pin 13 blinks as a heartbeat and has no effect on the trick.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: An Arduino Uno drives a milking parlour gate through two relay inputs: pin 5 opens and pin 6 shuts, and both must never be HIGH at the same time. A toggle push button on pin 2 (internal pullup, pressed = LOW) flips the wanted gate state, debounced at 50 ms, and the gate then runs toward that state until the matching limit switch on pin 3 (open) or pin 4 (shut) reads LOW, at which point both relays go LOW. A buzzer on pin 7 sounds 1000 Hz while opening and 700 Hz while shutting. Pins 0 and 1 are left alone for USB serial, which prints the new wanted state on each accepted press.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: Wire two LEDs (red to pin 8, green to pin 9) each through a 220 ohm resistor to ground, and wire a normally-open switch or IR detector between pin 2 and ground (the sketch enables the internal pull-up). When the sensor is pulled LOW (train present), the red LED turns on and the green LED turns off. After the sensor has been HIGH continuously for 5000 ms, the signal returns to green. The sketch prints state changes to serial at 9600 baud.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A DHT11 humidity sensor's data pin connects to Arduino D2 with a pull-up, a red LED with series resistor goes from D9 to ground, and a piezo buzzer sits on D8. The sketch samples humidity every 1000 ms and prints the reading to Serial at 9600 baud. If humidity exceeds 65 percent on 3 consecutive samples, the LED lights and the buzzer sounds a 2000 Hz tone; the alarm stays latched until a reading falls below 60 percent, which clears both outputs. Sensor read or checksum errors are reported on Serial and ignored.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: Wire a DHT22-style humidity sensor data line to D7, a relay module input to D9, and a momentary push button from D2 to ground. The relay is active-low, so D9 is driven HIGH at boot to keep the humidifier off. The sketch reads humidity every 2 seconds and turns the humidifier on when humidity drops below 88%, off when it rises above 93%, and always shuts it off after 120 seconds of continuous misting as a safety timeout. Holding the button forces misting on regardless of the reading.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: An Arduino Uno drives a roof motor through a relay on D9, reads an open limit switch on D2 and a closed limit switch on D3 (both wired to ground, using internal pull-ups), reads a normally-closed E-stop on D4, and shows status on the D13 LED. Over 9600-baud serial, sending 'o' starts opening only if the closed switch is active, 'c' starts closing only if the open switch is active, and 's' stops the motor immediately. The motor relay turns off when the target limit switch closes or after 45000 ms of travel, and while the E-stop is held low the motor is forced off and the LED blinks at 2 Hz.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A capacitive soil moisture sensor output feeds Arduino A0, a normally-open pushbutton connects D2 to ground, and a relay module driving the zone solenoid is on D9 with the onboard LED on D13. The sketch reads the soil every 2 seconds and opens the valve when the reading rises above 600, closing it again once the reading falls below 400, giving a 200-count hysteresis band. Holding the button forces the valve open regardless of moisture and releases it when the button is let go. The valve and LED are driven high to water and low to stop.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A 12V blower relay coil is driven through a transistor from D7, a Hall tach sensor pulls D2 low twice per revolution, a momentary button to ground is on D4 with the internal pull-up, and the onboard LED is on D13. Pressing the button toggles the blower; after a 4-second startup grace the firmware measures RPM once per second and trips a fault if RPM drops below 300, latching the relay off and blinking the LED at 2 Hz until the button is pressed again. A second check trips the fault if no tach edge has arrived for 1.5 seconds while running.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: An IR beam sensor module output is wired to Arduino pin 2 (internal pull-up enabled, active-low when a ball blocks the beam), and an indicator LED is on pin 13 through the built-in resistor. The sketch counts one ball each time the beam transitions from clear to blocked, ignoring repeat triggers within 40 ms, and prints 'Ball #N' over Serial at 9600 baud while blinking the LED for 5 ms per ball. The count is a 32-bit unsigned value starting at 0 and is never reset except by power cycle or reset button.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: Three LED channels are wired through 220-ohm resistors from Arduino PWM pins 9 (warm white), 10 (blue), and 11 (red) to ground, and a pushbutton connects pin 2 to ground using the internal pull-up. On power-up the dome starts dark, then continuously fades blue from 0 to 255 and back in steps of 5 with 40 ms per step, while warm white runs at half that brightness and red at one-eighth. Pressing the button toggles between the fading night-sky effect and all LEDs fully off, with a 300 ms debounce delay. The sketch uses only the Arduino core and ignores pins 0 and 1 so USB uploads keep working.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A Hall-effect sensor on D2 (internal pull-up, falling-edge interrupt) sees one pulse per magnet, with two magnets per wheel revolution. An 8-bit shift register (74HC595) is driven by D7 latch, D8 clock and D9 data, and its outputs feed a multiplexed 3-digit 7-segment display showing RPM. Every 500 ms the sketch counts pulses, converts to RPM as (pulses*60000/elapsed)/2, clamps the display to 999, and prints 'rpm=' plus the value to Serial at 9600 baud. Pulses closer than 2 ms apart are ignored as debounce.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: Wire a momentary trigger switch from Arduino pin 2 to GND (internal pull-up enabled), a relay or MOSFET pump control input to pin 8, and the onboard LED on pin 13 mirrors the pump. Pressing the trigger turns the pump on immediately; releasing it turns the pump off and starts a 5000 ms dwell during which the pump stays off and new presses are ignored. Input is debounced with a 30 ms window, and all timing uses millis() so the loop never blocks.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: Wire a photointerrupter sensor output to Arduino pin 2 (it reads LOW when a sheet blocks the beam) and a momentary reset button from pin 4 to GND using the internal pullup. Connect a 16x2 LCD in 4-bit mode with RS=7, E=8, D4=9, D5=10, D6=11, D7=12. The sketch must count falling edges on pin 2, ignore any pulse arriving less than 20 ms after the previous one, and show the running total on the LCD's second row. Holding the reset button clears the count to 0 and the display updates only when a new sheet is counted or a reset happens.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: Wiring: a pushbutton from pin 2 to GND (internal pull-up), a green LED with 220 ohm resistor from pin 8 to GND, a red LED with 220 ohm resistor from pin 9 to GND, and a piezo buzzer from pin 10 to GND. On power-up the green LED is on and the box is idle. Pressing the button starts a 10-second countdown: green goes off, red goes on, and the buzzer beeps 2 kHz for 60 ms once per second as the count decrements. Pressing the button again at any time aborts back to idle (green on, red off); when the count reaches zero both LEDs blink together every 250 ms until the button is pressed to reset.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A servo's signal wire goes to pin 9 and its horn is the brake arm; a beam-break or IR sensor with active-low output goes to pin 2 (internal pull-up enabled), and an indicator LED sits on pin 13. When the sensor goes LOW the sketch drives the servo to 90 degrees (brake applied), lights the LED, and prints a message over serial at 9600 baud. When the sensor returns HIGH it prints 'Train cleared' and turns the LED off, and the servo returns to 0 degrees (released) once 3 seconds have passed since the last detection. The loop polls every 10 ms.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A reed switch from D2 to GND (internal pull-up) reads closed/LOW when the anchor chain is taut; a mute button from D3 to GND is pressed/LOW to silence. style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: Wire a momentary push button between Arduino pin 2 and ground (internal pull-up enabled), a relay module input to pin 8, and an indicator LED to pin 13 through a 220 ohm resistor. Pressing the button toggles the heater relay on or off, with 50 ms of debounce so contact bounce is ignored. When the heater is turned on it may run for at most 30 minutes (1,800,000 ms), after which the firmware forces the relay off and the LED off until the button is pressed again. The relay output is active HIGH, so pin 8 goes HIGH to energize the heater and LOW to cut it.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: Guard interlock switch on D2 to ground (INPUT_PULLUP, HIGH means guard closed), start button on D3 to ground, stop button on D4 to ground, motor relay on D9, and status LED on D13. The motor only starts if the start button is held low continuously for at least 400 ms while the guard reads HIGH; releasing the button early cancels the start. Pressing stop (D4 low) stops the motor immediately. If the guard opens (D2 low) while running, the motor keeps running for up to 150 ms of grace and then shuts off; the LED mirrors the motor state.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: An ADXL335-style analog accelerometer output is wired to A0, with the Arduino's 5V and GND powering the module, and the onboard LED on D13 used as an event indicator. The sketch samples A0 every 10 ms (100 Hz) and maintains a slow baseline using a 1/64 IIR filter that only updates while no event is active. When the absolute deviation from baseline exceeds 40 ADC counts, it starts an event, tracks the peak deviation, and lights the LED; once the signal stays below threshold for 250 ms it prints 'EVENT t=<start ms> peak=<counts>' over Serial at 9600 baud and turns the LED off.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A 10k NTC thermistor sits between 5V and A0, with a 10k resistor from A0 to ground, and a 4-wire fan's PWM input goes to pin 9 (LED on pin 13). The sketch converts the A0 reading to Celsius with the Steinhart-Hart/B-parameter formula and maps 30-60 C to a PWM duty of 60-255, outputting 0 below 30 C and 255 at or above 60 C. Pin 13 lights whenever the temperature exceeds 50 C. Every 1000 ms it prints the temperature to Serial at 9600 baud in the form 'T=xx.xC PWM=nnn'.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A sewing machine foot pedal potentiometer wiper connects to A0 with its ends on 5V and GND, a motor driver PWM input goes to pin 9, and the onboard LED is on pin 13. The sketch averages 8 ADC samples, low-pass filters them, and maps 120..900 counts to PWM 0..255, treating anything at or below 120 as released. The motor only starts after the pedal reading has been stable for 150 ms and stops after it has been at zero for 400 ms, with the LED lit whenever the motor is driven. It prints the filtered reading, PWM value, and running flag over serial at 9600 baud every 250 ms.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: An HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor is wired with TRIG to D9 and ECHO to D10, a piezo buzzer on D6, a red LED on D7, and a toggle switch on D2 using INPUT_PULLUP so the alarm is armed when D2 reads LOW. The sketch pings the sensor every 200 ms and converts the echo to centimeters; if the measured distance is 40 cm or less it raises the alarm, and it only changes alarm state after at least 3000 ms since the last change. While armed and alarmed, the LED is held on and the buzzer toggles on and off every 400 ms; otherwise both outputs are driven LOW. Distance readings are printed to Serial at 9600 baud, and a zero-timeout echo is ignored.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: An IR break-beam sensor output is wired to pin 2 (INPUT_PULLUP, goes LOW when a skier breaks the beam), the onboard LED on pin 13, and a reset pushbutton from pin 7 to ground. Each HIGH-to-LOW transition on pin 2 increments a counter, prints 'Count: N' over serial at 9600 baud, and lights the LED for 100 ms. Pressing the reset button zeroes the count and prints 'Count reset'. The beam is debounced with a 50 ms delay after each count.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: Wire a 10k NTC thermistor (B=3950) from 5V to A0, with a 10k resistor from A0 to GND, so the thermistor is on the high side of the divider. Connect a relay module input to D9 (active HIGH) driving the heater, and a piezo buzzer to D8. It beeps once for 150 ms at 2 kHz when the target is first reached and prints temperature and heater state over Serial at 9600 baud once per second.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: Wire a relay module's signal input to Arduino pin 7, with the relay switching the tanning lamps' AC line (use a proper relay rated for the load; this is a low-voltage control signal only). When start is pressed and the lamps are off, the relay turns on and a 20-minute (1,200,000 ms) timer begins; when that timer expires the relay turns off. Pressing stop at any time turns the relay off immediately, and pressing start while already on is ignored.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A momentary foot pedal connects between Arduino D2 and GND (internal pullup used), and a 5V relay module signal input goes to D8 with the onboard LED on D13 mirroring it. Pressing the pedal energizes the relay so the tattoo machine runs; releasing it stops the machine. Two presses within 350 ms latch the relay on, and holding the pedal down for 1.5 seconds or more clears the latch and turns everything off. Input is debounced with a 25 ms window and status messages are printed at 9600 baud.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A 10k NTC thermistor sits in a divider with a 10k fixed resistor from 5V to A0, and a 12V heater strap is switched by an N-channel MOSFET whose gate is driven from pin 9 through a 220-ohm resistor. The sketch reads the thermistor every 500 ms, converts it to Celsius with the beta equation (beta 3950, 10k at 25C), and turns the heater on at 200/255 PWM when the strap drops below 11C and off when it rises above 13C. It prints temperature and heater state over Serial at 9600 baud and blinks the pin 13 LED once per second as a heartbeat.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A momentary pushbutton connects D2 to ground (internal pull-up enabled), and D9 drives the fog machine's remote trigger through a transistor, going HIGH to spray. Pressing the button starts a 3000 ms fog burst on D9, then the output goes LOW and a 5000 ms cooldown begins during which further presses are ignored. The onboard LED on D13 lights whenever D9 is HIGH. Button presses are debounced with a 30 ms timestamp filter.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A 10k NTC thermistor (beta 3950) sits in a divider with a 10k resistor from 5V to A0, thermistor from A0 to GND, sensing the basking spot. A relay module input connects to D7 and switches the basking lamp, active HIGH. Every 1000 ms the sketch averages 8 ADC samples, converts to Celsius via the beta equation, and turns the lamp ON below 30 C and OFF above 34 C, with a hard cutoff that keeps it OFF above 42 C. State and temperature are printed to Serial at 9600 baud.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A 16x2 LCD in 4-bit mode is wired to D12 (RS), D11 (EN), D5-D2 (D4-D7); a momentary button to D7 with internal pull-up (pressed = LOW), a piezo buzzer on D8, and an active-high relay on D9 driving the ultrasonic transducer. The LCD top line shows READY or CLEANING and the bottom line shows the selected time as M:SS, defaulting to preset index 1 (60 seconds) from the list 30/60/120/180/300/480 seconds. A short press starts the countdown (relay HIGH, display counts down, 40 ms beep on preset change) and a second short press stops it; holding the button longer than 700 ms while idle advances to the next preset with a 40 ms beep, and while running it aborts the cycle. When the countdown reaches zero the relay drops and the buzzer sounds three 150 ms beeps spaced 120 ms apart.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A0 reads a linear 10k thermistor divider mapped to -10..40 C; a reed anemometer on D2 pulls low once per revolution (interrupt on falling edge) and wind is considered OK if an edge arrived within the last 1500 ms. D7 drives the fan contactor relay and D13 mirrors it, while D4 is a momentary button to ground that toggles a manual override. In auto mode the fan starts only after temperature is at or below 2 C and wind is OK for a continuous 3 seconds, and stops when temperature reaches 5 C provided it has run at least 60 seconds. Serial at 9600 prints temperature, wind status, and run state every 200 ms.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: Wire an analog humidity sensor output to A0, and three LEDs with 220-ohm resistors from pins 8 (green), 9 (yellow), and 10 (red) to ground. Every 2 seconds the sketch reads A0 (0-1023), maps it linearly to 0-100 percent, and prints raw and percent values to Serial at 9600 baud. If humidity is below 35 percent only the red LED lights, from 35 to 44 percent only yellow lights, and at 45 percent or above only green lights. Exactly one LED is on at a time and it stays on until the next 2-second reading.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: Pin 9 drives a logic-level MOSFET gate that switches 5V through a nichrome wire; pin 13 has the onboard LED and pin 2 has a momentary button to ground using the internal pull-up. On boot the LED blinks three times at 150 ms on/off, then blinks once per second as a heartbeat. After 5,400,000 ms (90 minutes) or when the button is pressed, pin 9 goes HIGH for 4,000 ms to burn the cutter, then goes LOW, and the heartbeat speeds up to 200 ms. The cut only happens once; further button presses are ignored.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: A hobby servo's signal wire connects to Arduino pin 9, its power to 5V and ground to GND. A momentary pushbutton goes between pin 2 and GND (internal pull-up enabled), and the built-in LED on pin 13 indicates valve state. On power-up the servo moves to 0 degrees (valve closed) and the LED is off. Each button press toggles the valve between 0 degrees closed and 90 degrees open, moving the LED with it, with 50 ms debounce and a 500 ms settle delay after each move.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: An IR filament sensor output is wired to pin 2 with INPUT_PULLUP, so the pin reads LOW when filament is present and floats HIGH when the spool runs out. A piezo buzzer sits on pin 8 and the onboard LED on pin 13. The sketch debounces the sensor for 50 ms; when filament disappears it turns the LED on and beeps the buzzer 200 ms on, 800 ms off until filament is reloaded. Serial at 9600 baud prints 'Filament OK' and 'RUNOUT!' on state changes.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: The E-stop switch is wired between pin 2 and ground (internal pull-up), a relay coil driver sits on pin 7, a buzzer on pin 8, and the onboard LED on pin 13. The relay is energized (pin 7 HIGH) only while the machine is enabled; pressing the switch (pin 2 reads LOW for at least 25 ms) de-energizes the relay, sounds the buzzer, and blinks the LED at 2 Hz. The fault stays latched until the switch is released and held for 1500 ms, after which the relay re-energizes and the buzzer stops. Status messages are printed to Serial at 9600 baud.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: Wire a 2:1 resistor divider from the measured voltage to Arduino A0 so the pin never sees more than 5V, and connect six LEDs (with 220-ohm series resistors) from pins 2 through 7 to ground, pin 2 being the lowest LED. The sketch reads A0 every 100 ms, converts the 0-1023 reading to 0-5V, doubles it to recover the real 0-10V input, and lights one more LED for each 1.67V step. All six LEDs are on at 10V and all are off at 0V, and the raw value, voltage, and LED count are printed to Serial at 9600 baud.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A pushbutton connects pin 2 to ground (internal pull-up enabled) and a passive piezo buzzer sits on pin 8. When the button is held and released, the sketch measures the hold time: under 200 ms it plays a 120 ms 700 Hz tone (a dot), otherwise a 360 ms tone (a dash), printing '.' or '-' to serial at 9600 baud. After each tone it waits 120 ms of silence before the next element.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A 10k potentiometer is wired as a voltage divider with its ends to 5V and GND and its wiper to analog pin A0. An LED (with a 220 ohm series resistor) is connected from digital pin 9 to GND. The sketch reads the 10-bit ADC value (0-1023) about every 20 ms and maps it to a PWM duty cycle of 0-255 on pin 9, so the knob sweeps the LED from off to full brightness. Any ADC reading below 8 forces the output fully off, and the sketch prints the raw and mapped values over serial at 9600 baud only when the duty cycle changes.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A common-cathode RGB LED connects through three 220-ohm resistors to Arduino Uno pins 9 (red), 10 (green), 11 (blue), and a pushbutton ties pin 2 to ground using the internal pull-up. The sketch updates the LED every 20 ms and cycles through four modes on each button press (debounced at 250 ms): off, steady red, a 768-step color wheel advancing 3 steps per tick, and a 512-step white fade advancing 1 step per tick. Mode starts at 0 (off) after reset.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A 10k NTC thermistor is wired from A0 to GND with a 10k resistor from A0 to 5V, and a heater relay (via transistor) is driven from D7 with the onboard LED on D13 mirroring it. The sketch reads the thermistor with the beta equation (beta=3950, R0=10k at 25C) and turns the heater ON when temperature falls below 24.5C and OFF when it rises above 25.5C, giving a 1C hysteresis band around a 25C setpoint. If the computed temperature ever exceeds 35C the heater is forced OFF as a safety cutoff. It prints temperature and heater state over serial at 9600 baud once per second.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A TMP36 temperature sensor output feeds Arduino A0, a 5V fan relay is driven from digital pin 9, and the onboard LED on pin 13 mirrors the fan state. The sketch samples every 2000 ms, converts the ADC reading to millivolts (5V reference, 1024 counts) and then to Celsius using (mV-500)/10. The fan turns on when the temperature reaches 38 C or higher and turns off only after the temperature falls to 32 C or below AND the fan has been running for at least 60000 ms. Temperature readings are printed to Serial at 9600 baud.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor with TRIG on D9 and ECHO on D10, a pump relay on D6, and a status LED on D13. The sketch measures distance every ~60 ms and, when a hand is closer than 12 cm, runs the pump for 350 ms then enforces a 1200 ms cooldown before it can fire again. Distances are printed to Serial at 9600 baud; a pulseIn timeout of 25 ms is treated as 999 cm (no target).

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A 12V battery feeds a divider of 10k (R1) from the positive terminal to A0 and 4.7k (R2) from A0 to ground, so A0 sees about 0.38 of battery voltage; the on-board LED is on pin 13. Every 500 ms the sketch averages 16 analog samples, converts with a 5.0V/1023 reference, scales by (R1+R2)/R2, and prints 'Vbat=xx.xx OK/LOW/CRIT' at 9600 baud. Below 11.0V the LED blinks at 2 Hz, below 10.5V it toggles every 100 ms, and above 11.0V it stays off.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A TMP36 temperature sensor output feeds Arduino A0, powered from the 5V rail, and the onboard LED on D13 is used as a heartbeat. The sketch reads A0 every 60000 ms, converts the 0-1023 ADC count to volts using a 5.0 V reference, then to Celsius with the TMP36 formula (volts - 0.5) / 0.010. Each sample prints a CSV line 'millis,temp_c' at 9600 baud with two decimals, and blinks D13 high for 50 ms. A header row 'ms,temp_c' is printed once at startup.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A0 connects to the midpoint of a 10k/2.2k divider across the supply output, and A1 connects to the output of a x50 current-sense amplifier fed by a 0.1 ohm shunt, with D13 driving an overcurrent LED. The sketch averages 8 ADC samples per channel, converts them using a 5.0 V / 1023 reference, scales voltage by (12.2/2.2) and current by 5 V per amp, and prints 'V=xx.xx V  I=x.xxx A' over 9600 baud serial once per second. If the computed current exceeds 1.5 A, D13 is driven HIGH and ' [OCP]' is appended to the line; otherwise the LED is LOW.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: Two momentary push buttons connect from Arduino pins 2 and 3 to ground (internal pull-ups enabled), and two amber LEDs go from pins 8 and 9 through 220-ohm resistors to ground. Pressing the left button selects the left blinker, pressing it again cancels it; the right button does the same for the right blinker, and pressing one side while the other is active switches sides. The selected LED blinks on and off every 400 ms using millis(), while the unselected LED stays off. When nothing is selected both LEDs are held off.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: An IR beam-break sensor output is wired to pin 2 (with internal pull-up, so it reads LOW when a bottle blocks the beam), the onboard LED is on pin 13, and a momentary reset button connects pin 4 to ground. Each time the beam goes from clear to blocked, the sketch increments a counter, lights the LED while blocked, and prints 'Bottles: N' over serial at 9600 baud. Pressing the reset button sets the count back to 0 and prints 'Count reset'. A 30 ms debounce window ignores repeat triggers from the same bottle.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: Wire a 100k resistor from Arduino pin 2 to a 1uF capacitor whose other leg goes to GND, with pin 2 connected to the R-C junction. Every second the sketch drives pin 2 LOW for 50 ms to discharge the capacitor, then switches the pin to INPUT and times how long until it reads HIGH, expecting roughly 70 ms for a 0.1 s time constant. It prints the measured charge time in milliseconds over Serial at 9600 baud, or a TIMEOUT message if the pin stays LOW for more than 2000 ms.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: Wire a magnetic reed switch between Arduino pin 2 and GND, and a momentary pushbutton between pin 4 and GND; both pins use the internal pull-ups, so no external resistors are needed. Each time the reed switch closes (falling edge), the sketch increments a pass counter, ignoring any further edges within 300 ms to reject switch bounce. The count is printed to the Serial Monitor at 9600 baud as 'Passes: N' whenever it changes. Holding the button on pin 4 low for more than 50 ms resets the count to zero and prints 'Count reset' followed by 'Passes: 0'.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: An Arduino Uno drives a DC gear motor through an L293D H-bridge: pin 5 to input 1, pin 6 to input 2. Two normally-open limit switches connect pins 2 (top/fully open) and 3 (bottom/fully closed) to ground with internal pull-ups, and a pushbutton on pin 4 to ground toggles the door. A photocell voltage divider feeds A0; readings below 300 count as night and close the door, readings at or above 300 open it, but only while idle. Any motor run stops when its limit switch reads LOW or after 12000 ms, then the sketch pauses 250 ms and treats the door as open or closed accordingly.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: A sound sensor module's digital output is wired to Arduino pin 2, and an LED (or the onboard LED) is on pin 13. The sketch reads pin 2 each loop; when it goes HIGH and at least 300 ms have passed since the last accepted clap, it toggles the LED state and prints the new state over serial at 9600 baud. The LED starts OFF at power-up, and a single clap should flip it ON, with the next clap after the 300 ms window flipping it back OFF.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: Wire a slotted opto sensor to D2 (INPUT_PULLUP, pulses LOW once per shaft revolution), a motor relay to D7 (HIGH runs the motor), a red jam LED to D8, and a reset button from D9 to GND. On boot the motor runs and the LED is off; if no sensor pulse arrives for 1500 ms the sketch cuts the motor and latches the LED on. Pressing the reset button clears the jam and restarts the motor only if a pulse has been seen within the last 1500 ms, so a still-jammed belt stays stopped. Pulses are debounced with a 20 ms edge filter.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: A float switch is wired between Arduino pin 7 and ground, using the internal pull-up so pin 7 reads LOW when the bowl water is low. A relay module input connects to pin 9 and switches a small 5V pump; the relay is active-low, so pin 9 LOW turns the pump on and HIGH turns it off. When pin 7 reads LOW, the sketch turns the pump on for 4000 ms, then turns it off and waits 5000 ms for the water to settle before checking again. The pump never runs longer than 4 seconds per cycle, so a stuck-low float switch cannot flood the bowl indefinitely.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A momentary pushbutton connects between Arduino pin 2 and ground (internal pull-up enabled), and a piezo buzzer connects between pin 8 and ground. When the button is pressed, the sketch debounces it for 50 ms and then plays a two-note chime: 659 Hz for 400 ms followed by 523 Hz for 600 ms, then silences the buzzer. It ignores further presses until the button is released, and prints 'Ding'/'Dong' messages to Serial at 9600 baud.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A 16x2 HD44780 LCD is wired in 4-bit mode with RS=12, E=11, D4..D7=5,4,3,2; a momentary pushbutton to GND sits on pin 7 (internal pull-up), a piezo buzzer on pin 9, and the onboard LED on pin 13. The timer offers four presets of 180, 300, 420 and 600 seconds, shown as M:SS on the second LCD line; a short press starts or pauses the countdown, and a long press (over 800 ms) cycles to the next preset and resets the time. When the countdown reaches zero the LED blinks at 2 Hz and the buzzer beeps at 2000 Hz in half-second bursts until the button is short-pressed to reload the preset. While running the LED is solid on, and while paused or idle it is off.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: Six LEDs are wired from Arduino pins 3 through 8, each through a 220 ohm resistor to ground, and arranged as the pips of a die; a pushbutton connects pin 2 to ground (internal pull-up enabled). On power-up the sketch seeds the RNG from the floating analog pin A0 and displays face 1. When the button is pressed (debounced for 30 ms), the LEDs flash random faces every 70 ms for 900 ms, then settle on a final random face from 1 to 6. The sketch waits for the button to be released before accepting another roll.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A 3-floor elevator model uses a DC gearmotor driven by an L298N-style driver: IN1 on D4, IN2 on D5, and PWM enable on D6. Floor sensors for floors 1, 2, and 3 are on D7, D8, and D9 (active LOW), bottom and top limit switches are on D10 and D11 (active LOW), and call buttons for floors 1, 2, and 3 are on D2, D3, and D12 (active LOW, internal pull-ups). Pressing a call button sets that floor as the target; the cabin drives toward it at PWM 180 and stops when the matching floor sensor reads LOW, with limit switches cutting the motor if tripped. Buttons are debounced with a 30 ms delay, and the motor is stopped whenever the target equals the current floor.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A pushbutton connects pin 2 to ground (internal pull-up), a servo signal or feeder driver input goes to pin 9, an LED with resistor sits on pin 13, and a 10k potentiometer wiper feeds A0. The sketch feeds for 2 seconds every interval, defaulting to 480 minutes, and a short button press (40ms to 1.5s) triggers an immediate feed. Holding the button longer than 1.5 seconds reads the pot, maps it to 1 to 1440 minutes, and saves that interval to EEPROM addresses 0 and 1 so it survives power loss. The LED is lit while feeding, and serial at 9600 baud prints the interval and each feed event.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A 10k NTC thermistor sits in a voltage divider with a 10k resistor from 5V to A0, with the thermistor to ground. A piezo buzzer is on pin 8, a red LED on pin 9, and a momentary acknowledge button from pin 2 to ground using the internal pull-up. The sketch reads the temperature once per loop and, if it stays above -15 C for 60 seconds, lights the LED and sounds the buzzer. Pressing the acknowledge button silences the buzzer for 5 minutes while the LED stays on, and the alarm clears automatically once the temperature drops back to -15 C or below. Temperature is printed to Serial at 9600 baud once per second.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A normally-closed reed switch connects pin 2 to ground when the fridge door is shut, using the internal pull-up so the pin reads HIGH when open. A piezo buzzer sits on pin 8 (other leg to ground). After the door has been open continuously for 30000 ms, the buzzer beeps 200 ms on and 800 ms off until the door closes again. Closing the door immediately silences the buzzer and resets the timer.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: The toggle button connects pin 2 to ground (internal pull-up enabled), the 10k potentiometer wiper goes to A0 with its ends on 5V and GND, the fan MOSFET gate is driven from PWM pin 9, and the onboard LED on pin 13 shows status. Pressing the button toggles the fan on or off, debounced with a 30 ms window. When on, the pot's 0-1023 reading is mapped to a PWM duty of 40-255 on pin 9, and the status LED is lit; when off, pin 9 is driven to 0 and the LED is dark. Any computed duty below 40 is forced to 0 so the fan cannot stall at a low setting.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: An IR break-beam receiver output feeds Arduino pin 2 with INPUT_PULLUP, so the pin reads LOW when the beam is interrupted. Pin 8 drives a relay module that must be HIGH to permit the door to close and LOW to stop it, and pin 13 lights the onboard LED whenever the beam is broken. The sketch debounces the beam for 30 ms, immediately drops the relay and turns on the LED when the beam is blocked, and restores the relay when the beam is clear again. If the beam stays broken longer than 500 ms, the LED blinks at about 2 Hz as a warning.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: The MQ-2 analog output connects to Arduino A0 and a passive buzzer connects to digital pin 8 (through a transistor is fine). The sketch reads A0 every loop, prints the value over Serial at 9600 baud, and when the reading exceeds 400 it beeps the buzzer at 1000 Hz for 200 ms on and 200 ms off. Below the threshold it silences the buzzer and waits 500 ms between readings.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: An LM35 temperature sensor output feeds Arduino A0, a pushbutton connects pin 2 to ground (internal pull-up enabled), and pin 9 drives the vent motor through a transistor. The sketch reads the temperature every 500 ms and, when it exceeds 28 C with the vent closed, runs the motor for 8000 ms to open it; when temperature falls below 22 C with the vent open, it runs the motor 8000 ms to close it. Holding the button stops the motor immediately and skips the automatic logic until released. Serial output at 9600 baud prints the measured temperature in degrees C.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A PIR sensor output is wired to D2 and a relay-driven lamp to D9, with an LDR divider on A0. The sketch polls the PIR every 50 ms and, when motion is seen and the LDR reads below 400 (dark), turns the lamp on and restarts a 30-second hold timer. The lamp stays on until 30 seconds pass with no new motion, then turns off. A 40-count hysteresis band around the 400 threshold prevents the light/dark decision from chattering.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: An IR reflective sensor on D2 pulls LOW when a hand is within about 5 cm; D9 drives a MOSFET that powers a 5V peristaltic pump, and D13 lights the onboard LED while pumping. The sketch must wait until the hand has been continuously detected for 50 ms, then run the pump for 400 ms to dispense one dose. After each dose it must ignore the sensor for at least 1500 ms and require the hand to be removed before another dose can start. The pump output is active HIGH and idles LOW.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: Wire a TMP36-style analog temperature sensor output to A0, a piezo buzzer to digital pin 8, and a green LED (with a 220 ohm resistor) to digital pin 7.
