If the temperature is above 40 C or below 30 C, the buzzer sounds a 1 kHz tone and the green LED stays off; otherwise the buzzer is silent and the green LED is on. Debug text is printed to Serial at 9600 baud.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A DHT22 humidity/temperature sensor is wired to Arduino pin 2 (with its data line pulled up to 5V), and a relay module controlling the bathroom fan is driven from pin 8, with the onboard LED on pin 13 mirroring fan state. The sketch reads humidity every 2 seconds and turns the fan on when humidity rises above 65%, then turns it off only after humidity falls below 55% and the fan has been running for at least 120 seconds. Sensor read failures are printed to serial at 9600 baud and skipped. The relay is active-high, so pin 8 goes HIGH to run the fan.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: An L298N motor driver is wired with IN1 to D8 and IN2 to D9, driving a 12V geared DC motor that rocks the egg tray; the onboard LED on D13 lights while the motor runs. Every 7200000 ms (2 hours) the sketch runs the motor for 4000 ms, alternating direction each cycle so the tray tilts one way then the other. The motor is stopped (both inputs LOW) between turns, and the first turn happens 2 hours after power-up. No limit switches or sensors are used, so turn duration is fixed by timing alone.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: An Arduino Uno drives a 16x2 LCD in 4-bit mode with RS on D12, E on D11, and data lines on D5, D4, D3, D2; three momentary buttons to ground with internal pull-ups sit on D6 (up), D7 (down), and D8 (start/stop), and a piezo buzzer is on D9. The timer boots showing a 5:00 set time on the second LCD line; pressing up adds 30 seconds and down subtracts 30 seconds, clamped between 0:30 and 99:59. Pressing start copies the set time into the countdown, decrements it once per second, and shows it as MM:SS; pressing start again pauses. When the count reaches zero the first line shows DONE! and the buzzer sounds five 2 kHz beeps of 300 ms separated by 200 ms gaps, then the display returns to the set time.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: Wire a lid microswitch from D2 to GND (closed lid = LOW), an arm button from D3 to GND, and a reset button from D4 to GND, all using the internal pull-ups. Connect D8 to the laser enable input, D9 to a piezo buzzer, D10 to a green LED, and D11 to a red LED, each through a 220 ohm resistor to GND. Pressing arm while the lid is closed sets D8 HIGH and lights green; opening the lid while armed immediately drives D8 LOW, latches a fault, lights red, and sounds a 1 kHz tone on D9. Pressing reset with the lid closed clears the fault and silences the buzzer.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A 10k potentiometer's wiper goes to A0 with ends on 5V and GND, a pushbutton connects D2 to GND (internal pull-up used), a piezo buzzer sits on D8, and the onboard LED on D13 is used. The pot sets tempo from 40 to 240 BPM (0-1023 maps linearly), and pressing the button toggles the metronome on or off. While running, every beat interval (60000/BPM ms) the sketch plays a 2000 Hz tone on the piezo for 15 ms and lights the LED for the same 15 ms. When stopped, the LED stays off and no clicks are produced.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: Wire an HC-SR04 with TRIG to D9 and ECHO to D10, and a passive buzzer on D8. The sketch triggers a 10 microsecond pulse every loop, measures the echo with a 30 ms timeout, and converts to centimeters by dividing by 58. If the distance is under 10 cm it beeps at 2000 Hz with 80 ms on/off, under 30 cm at 1500 Hz with 120 ms on and 250 ms off, under 60 cm at 1000 Hz with 100 ms on and 600 ms off, and otherwise stays silent. A missing echo (timeout) is treated as no obstacle and keeps the buzzer quiet.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: An IR photo-gate output is wired to D2 with the internal pull-up enabled, so the line idles HIGH and goes LOW when the beam is blocked; the onboard LED is on D13. A FALLING interrupt on D2 timestamps the beam break with micros(), and the sketch reports the block duration in microseconds over Serial at 115200 baud, flashing D13 for 50 ms per event. If the beam stays blocked longer than 2 seconds it prints 'timeout' and re-arms. The sketch prints 'photo gate ready' once at boot.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: Wire a target switch from Arduino pin 2 to ground and a bumper switch from pin 3 to ground; both pins use the internal pull-up so they read HIGH when open. The sketch prints a startup message at 9600 baud, then adds 100 points each time pin 2 goes from open to closed and 250 points each time pin 3 does, printing the points added and the running total. It only scores on the transition to pressed, so holding a switch does not keep adding points, and it polls every 10 ms.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A 5V relay module signal input connects to Arduino pin 7, its VCC and GND to the Uno's 5V and GND, and a 10k potentiometer wiper goes to A0 with its ends on 5V and GND. The sketch keeps a simple hour counter that starts at 0 on boot and increments every 3600 seconds, and reads the pot to set the light-on hour from 0 to 23 (off is always 12 hours later, wrapping past midnight). The relay is driven HIGH whenever the current hour falls in the on window, otherwise LOW, and every 5 seconds it prints hour, on-hour, off-hour, and light state over Serial at 9600 baud.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A 5V relay module signal input connects to D7, the pump's switched live runs through the relay's NO contacts, and two momentary pushbuttons to GND sit on D8 (set ON time) and D9 (set OFF time) using internal pull-ups. A 10k potentiometer wiper feeds A0 and sets the time in minutes (0-1439) that gets stored when a button is pressed; settings persist in EEPROM behind a magic word. The sketch keeps a software clock from millis() and energizes the relay whenever the current minute-of-day falls inside the ON/OFF window, handling windows that wrap past midnight. The onboard LED on D13 blinks once per second while the pump is on and four times per second while it is off.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: Four active-low pushbuttons on pins 2-5 (internal pull-ups) and four LEDs on pins 8-11; a piezo buzzer on pin 12, a reset button on pin 6, and an arm button on pin 7. Pressing arm enables the round; the first button pressed lights its LED, sounds the buzzer at 1000 Hz plus 200 Hz per player for 300 ms, and locks out all others. Reset clears the lockout, LEDs, and buzzer. Serial prints 'WIN n' at 9600 baud when a player wins.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: Two IR break-beam sensors feed D2 (approach A) and D3 (exit B), active-low with internal pull-ups. D8/D9/D10 drive red, amber and green LEDs through 220 ohm resistors, D6 drives a piezo buzzer, and D5 drives a servo signal line (HIGH = gate down). When A breaks, the green LED goes off, amber lights for 1.5 s, then the gate drops and the red LED plus buzzer blink together at 400 ms intervals until B breaks. If no sensor edge occurs for 20 s while a train is present, the crossing resets to green with the gate up.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A tipping-bucket rain gauge reed switch connects between Arduino pin 2 and ground, using the internal pull-up, and the onboard LED on pin 13 is used as a blink indicator. Each switch closure (falling edge) counts one bucket tip of 0.2794 mm, debounced in software to ignore edges within 50 ms of the previous tip. Every 5000 ms the sketch prints 'tips=<count> mm=<count*0.2794>' over serial at 9600 baud, but only when the count has changed since the last report, and blinks the LED for 20 ms on each new report.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: An LED is connected from pin 8 through a 220 ohm resistor to ground, and a pushbutton connects pin 2 to ground (internal pull-up enabled). Pressing the button starts a round: the LED stays off for a random 1000 to 4000 ms, then turns on and the sketch records the time. When the player presses the button again, the LED turns off and the reaction time in milliseconds is printed to Serial at 9600 baud. The sketch then waits for the next button press to start another round.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: A single hobby servo's signal wire connects to Arduino pin 9, with its power on 5V and ground on GND. The sketch sweeps the servo from 0 to 180 degrees and back, moving 1 degree every 15 ms, so a full one-way sweep takes about 2.7 seconds. On startup it first moves to 90 degrees and waits 500 ms before sweeping. If the servo buzzes or the board resets, the servo should be powered from a separate 5V supply with a shared ground.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A pushbutton connects pin 2 to ground (internal pull-up enabled), a status LED with series resistor sits on pin 13, and a piezo buzzer is on pin 9. A short press starts a 300-second shower timer: the LED blinks once per second and a brief 2 kHz beep sounds at start. At 240 seconds the LED switches to blinking every 200 ms and a 300 ms warning beep sounds; at 300 seconds the timer stops, the LED goes off, and three 150 ms beeps at 2.5 kHz play. Pressing the button again while running cancels the timer immediately.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: An MQ-2 smoke sensor analog output feeds Arduino A0, a relay module signal input is on D7, and the onboard LED is on D13. The sketch reads A0 every 50 ms and, when the reading stays above 400 (on the 0-1023 scale) continuously for 2000 ms, it drives D7 and D13 HIGH to trip the relay and light the LED. When the reading drops back to 400 or below, it immediately drives D7 and D13 LOW and prints a clear message over serial at 9600 baud.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A capacitive soil moisture sensor output goes to analog pin A0 and a relay module controlling the irrigation valve is driven from digital pin 7 (HIGH = valve open, LOW = closed). The sketch averages 8 ADC samples every 2 seconds and maps raw counts from 620 (dry, 0%) to 280 (wet, 100%), clamped to 0-100. It opens the valve when moisture drops below 30% and closes it once moisture rises above 55%, and it force-closes the valve if it has been open for 2 minutes continuously. Status messages are printed to Serial at 9600 baud.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A 12V solar panel and battery feed a 10k/4.7k divider from battery positive to ground, with the midpoint on A0; the load is switched by a relay module on D8 (HIGH = load on) and D13 drives a status LED. The sketch samples A0 eight times, converts to battery volts using a 5.0V reference and the 3.128 divider ratio, and turns the load off when the reading drops below 11.8V. It turns the load back on only after the battery rises above 12.6V, and blinks D13 every 500ms while the load is off. Readings and state changes are printed to Serial at 9600 baud.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: An electret microphone module with analog output feeds Arduino A0, and five LEDs with 220-ohm resistors connect from pins 2 through 6 to ground. The sketch samples A0 as fast as possible for 50 ms, takes the largest absolute deviation from the 512 midpoint, and smooths that peak with a 3:1 running average. It lights 0 to 5 LEDs by mapping the smoothed level from 20 to 900 onto the bar, and prints the level to Serial at 9600 baud every 250 ms.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: The stepper is a 200-step-per-revolution bipolar motor driven through a ULN2003-style board: Arduino pins 8, 9, 10 and 11 connect to the four motor coils in order. Three momentary pushbuttons tie pins 2 (forward), 3 (reverse) and 4 (fast) to ground and use the internal pull-ups, so a press reads LOW. Pressing forward alone steps the motor one step forward per loop; pressing reverse alone steps it one step backward; pressing both does nothing. Holding the fast button raises the step rate from 30 to 120 steps per second and lights the onboard LED on pin 13, otherwise the LED is off and the rate is 30 steps per second.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A float switch connects between Arduino pin 2 and ground (internal pull-up enabled), so pin 2 reads LOW when the sump water is high. A pump relay coil driver is on pin 8, a piezo buzzer on pin 9, and the onboard LED on pin 13. When the float goes high the pump and LED turn on; the pump stays on at least 5000 ms after the float drops and is forced off after 60000 ms of continuous running. If the float remains high for 90000 ms the buzzer sounds until the float drops.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A hall-effect sensor with open-collector output is wired to D2 (internal pull-up enabled) and its output pulses are counted on each falling edge; a PWM indicator LED or meter is driven from D9 through a 220-ohm resistor. The sensor is assumed to produce 2 pulses per revolution. Every 1000 ms the sketch computes RPM from the pulse count in that window, blends in an instantaneous estimate from the last measured edge period (60,000,000 / (period_us * 2)), and prints 'RPM: <value>  pulses: <count>' at 115200 baud. It also writes analogWrite(D9) = rpm/4, clamped to 0-255, so 1000 RPM gives about 250 PWM counts.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A 10k NTC thermistor connects from 5V to analog pin A0, with a 10k resistor from A0 to GND, forming a voltage divider. The sketch averages 8 ADC samples, converts the divider voltage to resistance and then to Celsius using the Beta equation (Beta=3950, nominal 10k at 25C), and prints a CSV line of 'time_ms,temp_c' at 9600 baud once per second. The onboard LED on pin 13 goes high during each sample and low afterward. Readings below 0.01V or above 4.99V are clamped to -99C and 150C respectively to avoid divide-by-zero.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A single LED (through a suitable driver) is connected to Arduino pin 9, and a pushbutton to ground is wired to pin 2 using the internal pull-up. On power-up the sketch waits 60 seconds, then fades the LED from 0 to full brightness (PWM 0 to 255) over 30 minutes, updating once per second. Pressing the button starts the same 30-minute fade immediately, and after the fade completes the LED stays at full brightness until reset.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: Three LEDs are wired to digital pins 8 (red), 9 (yellow/amber) and 10 (green), each through a 220 ohm resistor to ground. The sketch runs a repeating UK-style cycle: red alone for 5000 ms, red plus amber for 1000 ms, green alone for 5000 ms, then amber alone for 2000 ms before returning to red. All timing uses blocking delay() calls, so the sequence is fixed and the loop repeats forever.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: Wire two momentary pushbuttons from pins 2 and 3 to ground, using the Arduino's internal pull-ups so each reads LOW when pressed. Connect LEDs through 220-ohm resistors from pins 8 and 9 to ground, and use the onboard LED on pin 13 as the win indicator. Each new press of player 1's button adds one point to score1, and each new press of player 2's button adds one to score2; holding a button must not add extra points. The first player to reach 10 points wins, after which the pin 13 LED blinks at 200 ms on/off forever and no more points are counted.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: An IR beam-break coin sensor output is wired to Arduino pin 2 with the internal pull-up enabled, so the pin reads HIGH when clear and LOW when a coin blocks the beam. The onboard LED on pin 13 blinks for 50 ms each time a coin is detected. The sketch counts one coin per HIGH-to-LOW transition, prints the running total over Serial at 9600 baud, and ignores repeated LOW readings so a single coin is not counted many times. A 10 ms loop delay limits how fast the sensor is sampled.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A reed switch anemometer is wired between Arduino pin D2 and ground, using the internal pull-up, so each cup half-turn closes the switch and triggers a falling-edge interrupt. An LED with a resistor sits on pin D13 to ground. The sketch counts pulses in an interrupt, then every 2000 ms converts the count to speed using 2.4 km/h per pulse per second and prints 'Pulses: N  Wind: X.X km/h' at 9600 baud. The D13 LED is lit whenever a pulse arrived within the last 500 ms, otherwise off.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A reed switch connects D2 to GND (internal pull-up enabled) so the pin reads LOW when the window is shut and HIGH when open. A piezo buzzer sits between D8 and GND. After the window has been continuously open for 10 seconds, the buzzer emits a 100 ms chirp once every 1000 ms until the window closes again. Openings shorter than 10 seconds produce no sound, and switch changes are debounced over 50 ms.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: An Arduino Uno drives a 5V relay on D7 that powers a 12V RO top-off pump, with a status LED on D13. Two float switches wired to GND use internal pull-ups: D2 is the low-level switch (LOW means the sump needs water) and D3 is the high-level overfill cutoff (LOW means stop). When D2 reads LOW and D3 reads HIGH, the sketch turns the pump on, but never for more than 60000 ms continuously, and after any run it waits at least 30000 ms before starting again. If D3 ever reads LOW the pump is switched off immediately regardless of state.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: Wire the leak sensor board's VCC to 5V, GND to GND, and its D0 digital output to Arduino pin 2; ignore the A0 pin. Connect a piezo buzzer from pin 9 to GND (through a transistor if it draws more than about 20 mA), and put a red LED with a 220 ohm resistor from pin 13 to GND. The sketch polls pin 2 every 100 ms and treats HIGH as water; it must see the sensor stay wet continuously for 2000 ms before alarming. Once alarmed, the LED on pin 13 goes solid on and the buzzer on pin 9 beeps at 500 ms on, 500 ms off until the sensor reads dry again, at which point the alarm clears automatically.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A Hall-effect sensor (A3144, open collector) is wired to D2 with the internal pull-up, a magnet on the drive wheel gives one LOW pulse per revolution, and an active-low relay board on D7 drives the saw motor. A normally-closed reset button connects D8 to ground. At boot the relay is off; pressing the button enables the motor, and while running the sketch expects a pulse at least every 1500 ms (about 0.5 s per revolution at full speed). If no pulse arrives within 1500 ms the relay is dropped and a FAULT line is printed at 9600 baud; a later pulse or a button press re-arms it.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A BMP280 barometer sits on I2C at address 0x76 (SDA to A4, SCL to A5 on the Uno), and a status LED with a series resistor is on pin 9. The sketch configures the sensor for normal mode and reads the raw 20-bit pressure register every 2 seconds. It computes the change in raw pressure since the previous sample and maps that delta to a PWM brightness on pin 9, centered at 128 and clamped to 0-255, so a rising pressure trend brightens the LED and a falling trend dims it. The initial reading is stored as a baseline but is not otherwise used.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A radon sensor's analog output feeds Arduino A0, a 5V relay module driving the basement fan is on D9, a status LED is on D13, and a momentary button to ground is on D2 with the internal pull-up enabled. Every 5 seconds the sketch averages 8 ADC samples; if the fan is off and the average exceeds 420 counts it turns the fan on, and if the fan is on and the average drops below 300 counts it turns the fan off, but only after the fan has run at least 60 seconds. Pressing the button toggles the fan manually regardless of sensor readings, and the LED mirrors the fan state. Readings and fan changes are printed to Serial at 9600 baud.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A piezo buzzer connects to Arduino pin 8 and a pushbutton goes from pin 2 to ground using the internal pullup, with the onboard LED on pin 13. Pressing the button toggles between locked and unlocked: unlocking plays a 1000 Hz beep for 100 ms then a 1500 Hz beep for 100 ms and turns the LED on, while locking plays a single 600 Hz beep for 200 ms and turns the LED off. Presses within 300 ms are ignored as debounce. While unlocked it emits a 2000 Hz, 40 ms chirp every 5 seconds, and status messages are printed at 9600 baud.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A PIR motion sensor output connects to Arduino D2 and reads HIGH on motion, a camera shutter relay connects to D7 and is active LOW (LOW presses the shutter), and the onboard LED on D13 mirrors the shutter pulse. On boot the sketch waits 30000 ms for the PIR to settle, then polls D2 continuously. When motion is seen and at least 5000 ms have passed since the last shot, it pulls D7 LOW for 150 ms to trip the shutter, lights D13 for that same pulse, then releases the relay and waits out the cooldown before it can fire again.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A 10k NTC thermistor divider feeds A0 (5V through 10k to A0, thermistor A0 to GND), a heater relay coil is driven from D9 through a transistor, a fan relay from D8, and the onboard LED on D13 mirrors the heater. The sketch reads temperature every 0.5 s using the linear approximation (V-0.5)*100, runs a PID (Kp=40, Ki=0.8, Kd=120) with integral clamped to +/-50, and forces the heater off whenever the PID output is non-positive. A 0.5 C hysteresis band around the 27.0 C setpoint latches the heater on below 26.5 C and off above 27.5 C, and the fan runs whenever the heater is on. Temperature and PID output are printed to Serial at 9600 baud.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: Wire a 10k NTC thermistor from A0 to GND and a 10k fixed resistor from 5V to A0, forming a divider; connect a piezo buzzer from D8 to GND. The sketch samples A0 every 500 ms, converts the divider voltage to resistance and then to Celsius with the beta equation (beta 3950, 10k at 25 C), and prints the temperature to Serial at 9600 baud. When the reading reaches 150 C the alarm latches and D8 beeps 150 ms on, 350 ms off; it clears only after the temperature falls below 147 C.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: A 12V car battery feeds a two-resistor voltage divider into Arduino A0 (the sketch assumes a 2:1 ratio, so 12V becomes 6V at the pin, which is actually over the 5V limit and should be fixed with a 10k/3.3k divider). A buzzer on pin 7 sounds when the measured voltage falls below 11.8V and turns off once it rises above 12.2V, giving a 0.4V hysteresis band. Pin 13 toggles as a heartbeat LED, and the sketch prints the raw ADC value and computed battery voltage to serial at 9600 baud every 500ms. The ADC is assumed to use the default 5V reference with 1024 steps.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: A TMP36 temperature sensor output feeds Arduino A0, powered from 5V, and a hobby servo's signal wire connects to pin 9 with its own 5V and ground. The sketch reads the sensor every 2 seconds, converts the 0-1023 reading to Celsius using the TMP36 0.5V offset and 10mV/C slope, and prints the temperature to Serial at 9600 baud. When the temperature rises above 28 C the servo moves from 0 degrees (lid closed) to 90 degrees (lid open), and when it falls below 24 C the servo returns to 0 degrees, giving 4 C of hysteresis so the lid does not flap. The lid state is remembered in a boolean so the servo only moves on a threshold crossing.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: A TMP36 temperature sensor's output pin goes to Arduino A0, powered from 5V and GND. A fan (or LED for testing) is driven from pin 9 through a transistor, and the built-in LED on pin 13 mirrors the fan state. Every 2000 ms the sketch reads A0, converts the 0-1023 reading to volts (5.0 V reference) and then to Celsius using C = (V - 0.5) * 100, and prints raw and temperature over serial at 9600 baud. The fan turns on when the temperature reaches 65.0 C or higher and turns off only when it drops to 60.0 C or lower, providing 5 C of hysteresis.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A 12V dehydrator fan is driven through a MOSFET on pin 9 and a 12V heater element through a relay on pin 8, with a momentary pushbutton to ground on pin 2 (internal pull-up) and the onboard LED on pin 13. A TMP36 temperature sensor output feeds analog pin A0, read once per second and converted at 10mV per degree C. Pressing the button toggles the run: when running, the fan and LED turn on and the heater switches on below 52C and off above 58C (target 55C with 3C hysteresis). The run automatically stops after 6 hours, turning off fan, heater, and LED.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: An HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor is wired with VCC to 5V, GND to GND, TRIG to Arduino pin 9, and ECHO to pin 10; an LED with a series resistor connects from pin 13 to GND. Every 200 ms the sketch sends a 10 microsecond trigger pulse and measures the echo pulse width with a 30 ms timeout, converting it to centimeters using 0.0343 cm per microsecond divided by two. If the measured distance is greater than 0 and less than 70 cm, pin 13 is driven HIGH to indicate the desk is occupied; otherwise it is driven LOW. The measured distance is printed to Serial at 9600 baud for debugging.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A reed switch connects pin 2 to ground when a magnet is near (drawer closed), using the internal pull-up so the pin reads HIGH when the drawer is open. Pin 13 drives an LED that is on whenever the drawer is considered open. The sketch debounces the switch for 50 ms, prints 'OPEN #n' on each opening and 'CLOSED after X ms' on each closing, and while open prints a status line every 1000 ms showing current open duration and accumulated total open time. Serial runs at 9600 baud.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: An Arduino Uno reads a quadrature rotary encoder on D2/D3 with internal pull-ups; each detent is 0.5 mm of quill travel. A momentary button on D4 to ground zeroes the depth reading, and D13 lights when depth reaches the 25.0 mm target. A 16x2 LCD in 4-bit mode (RS D7, EN D8, data D9-D12) shows current depth on line 1 and the target on line 2, refreshed at least every 20 ms. The encoder is decoded in pin-change interrupts and the count is read atomically in the main loop.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: The fence sense line goes to D2 with the internal pull-up enabled, so each negative-going pulse from the fence energizer pulls D2 low and triggers a falling-edge interrupt. A status LED sits on D13 through its usual series resistor, and a piezo buzzer is on D8. The sketch counts pulses, records the gap in milliseconds between the last two pulses, and every second prints 'pulses=', total count, 'rate=', pulses in the last second, and 'gap=' to serial at 9600 baud. If no pulse has arrived for more than 3 seconds it beeps the buzzer at 1000 Hz for 50 ms and blinks the LED as a fault warning, and the LED is held on whenever the most recent gap was under 200 ms.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A normally-open pushbutton connects pin 2 to ground (internal pull-up enabled), a passive piezo buzzer sits on pin 9, and the onboard LED is on pin 13. When the button is pressed and debounced for 25 ms, the sketch plays a two-tone chime: 880 Hz for 400 ms, a 120 ms gap, then 1320 Hz for 400 ms, with the LED lit for the whole chime. Further presses are ignored for 3 seconds after a chime starts, and each chime logs 'chime' over serial at 9600 baud.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A normally-open pushbutton connects D2 to ground (internal pull-up enabled), a 5V relay module signal input goes to D8, and the onboard LED on D13 is used as an indicator. Pressing the button energizes the relay and lights the LED for exactly 5000 ms, then both turn off; presses during the hold are ignored. Button reads are debounced with a 30 ms window, and the sketch prints 'open' and 'close' over serial at 9600 baud.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A 48V golf cart pack feeds a 100k/10k divider whose midpoint goes to A0, giving a divide-by-11 so 53V reads about 4.8V at the pin. Ten LEDs on D2 through D11 light as a bar graph, one per threshold from 40.0V up to 53.0V in roughly 1-1.5V steps. The sketch reads A0 against the 5.0V reference, multiplies by 11, smooths with a 0.9/0.1 low-pass, and lights all bars whose threshold the smoothed voltage meets or exceeds, updating every 200ms and printing the voltage to serial at 9600 baud.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A DHT22 temperature sensor is wired to Arduino pin D2 with its data line pulled up, a heater relay control input is on pin D7, and a status LED is on pin D13. The sketch reads the temperature once per second and turns the heater ON when the reading drops below 18.0 C, then OFF once it rises above 20.0 C, using that 2-degree hysteresis band to avoid relay chatter. If the DHT22 read returns NaN, the heater is forced ON as a fail-safe and the sketch waits 5 seconds before retrying. Each cycle prints the temperature to serial at 9600 baud along with the current heater state.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A soil moisture sensor output feeds analog pin A0, a relay module controlling the mister pump is on digital pin 7, and the onboard LED on pin 13 mirrors the pump state. The sketch reads the sensor every 2000 ms and prints the raw value to Serial at 9600 baud. When the reading rises above 600 (dry) it turns the relay and LED on, and when the reading falls below 400 (wet) it turns them off, giving a 200-count hysteresis band. The pump stays in its current state between checks, so it never chatters on a single borderline reading.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A small DC hand-crank generator's output goes through a 3:1 resistor divider into A0, and a magnet-and-reed/hall sensor on the crank shaft pulls D2 low once per pass (INPUT_PULLUP, RISING interrupt). The Arduino Uno averages 8 ADC samples, converts to volts using a 5.0 V reference and the 3x divider, and once per second prints voltage, pulses per second, and RPM (2 pulses per revolution) over Serial at 9600 baud. D13 lights when the measured voltage exceeds 6.0 V. Readings are smoothed and the loop runs about every 50 ms plus sampling time.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: Wire an analog temperature sensor output to A0 (10 mV per degree C, 0 V at -10 C), a compressor relay control input to digital pin 7, and a circulation pump relay to digital pin 8. The sketch reads the sensor every loop and turns the compressor on when the water rises above 3.5 C, but only if it has been off for at least 180 seconds; it turns the compressor off when the water falls below 2.5 C, but only after at least 60 seconds of run time. The pump runs whenever the compressor runs and continues for 15 seconds after the compressor stops. Every 1000 ms it prints the temperature, compressor state, and pump state over serial at 9600 baud.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: Three relay inputs controlling sprinkler valves are wired to Arduino Uno digital pins 4, 5, and 6, with the relays active HIGH. On power-up all three pins are driven LOW so no valve opens. The sketch runs zone 1 for 10 seconds, waits 2 seconds, runs zone 2 for 10 seconds, waits 2 seconds, runs zone 3 for 10 seconds, waits 2 seconds, then pauses 60 seconds before repeating forever. Serial output at 9600 baud prints each zone change for monitoring only.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A normally-open microswitch on the crane's upper limit is wired between D2 and GND, using the internal pull-up so D2 reads LOW when the hook reaches the top. D7 and D8 drive two active-high relay inputs for the up and down motors, and D13 lights an LED while either motor runs. The sketch listens on serial at 9600 baud: sending 'u' runs the up relay until the limit switch closes or 4000 ms elapse, and sending 'd' runs the down relay until any serial byte arrives or 4000 ms elapse. The switch is debounced with a 25 ms window, and any stop prints either LIMIT or TIMEOUT to serial.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: Wire a normally-open microswitch between pin 2 and GND (internal pull-up enabled), an LED with a 220 ohm resistor from pin 13 to GND, and a piezo buzzer from pin 9 to GND. The switch reads LOW when the mailbox flag is raised. On a debounced LOW transition the sketch turns the LED on and plays a 1000 Hz tone for 200 ms; on a HIGH transition it turns the LED off and silences the buzzer. Debounce time is 50 ms and the loop polls every 5 ms.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A normally-open pedal switch connects between Arduino pin 2 and ground, using the internal pull-up, and a reset button connects pin 7 to ground the same way. The built-in LED on pin 13 flashes for 60 ms each time a pedal press is counted, and every new count is printed to Serial at 9600 baud as 'count=N'. Presses are debounced in the interrupt handler with a 25 ms window, and pressing the reset button zeroes the count and prints 'reset'. The counter is a volatile unsigned long incremented in a falling-edge ISR on pin 2.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A hobby servo's signal wire goes to D9, its power to 5V and ground to GND; a photoresistor divider (10k fixed resistor to ground) feeds A0; the onboard LED on D13 indicates locked state. The sketch reads A0 every 100 ms and treats readings above 400 as daylight. Daylight must persist for 5000 ms before the servo moves from 20 degrees (locked) to 110 degrees (open), and darkness must persist 5000 ms before it returns to 20 degrees. D13 is HIGH while locked and LOW while open, and status messages print to Serial at 9600 baud.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A K-type thermocouple amplifier output feeds analog pin A0 (10 mV per degree C, 0.5 V offset), a momentary button to ground is on pin 7 with the internal pull-up, a relay module control input is on pin 8, a piezo buzzer is on pin 9, and a 16x2 LCD is wired in 4-bit mode with RS=12, EN=11, D4=5, D5=4, D6=3, D7=2. The sketch reads temperature every 500 ms and turns the relay on when the reading is more than 5 C below the setpoint and off when more than 5 C above it, displaying temperature and setpoint on the LCD. Each button press adds 10 C to the setpoint, wrapping from 400 C back to 150 C, starting at 250 C. If the temperature ever exceeds the setpoint by 20 C the buzzer sounds for about 300 ms as an over-temperature warning, and the warning re-arms once the temperature drops below the setpoint.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: A relay module controlling the aerator pump is wired to Arduino pin 7 (active-LOW: LOW energizes the relay), and the onboard LED on pin 13 blinks once per second as a heartbeat. On power-up the sketch immediately turns the pump ON and keeps it on for 28800 seconds (8 hours), then turns it OFF for 57600 seconds (16 hours), repeating that 8-on/16-off cycle forever using millis() timing. There is no real-time clock, so the schedule restarts from zero whenever the board resets or loses power. The loop polls every 50 ms and flips the relay state when the current phase's elapsed time reaches its limit.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A 12V 4-wire PC fan's PWM wire goes to Arduino pin 9 (fan ground tied to Arduino ground), a DHT22 data pin to pin 2 with a 10k pull-up to 5V, and a momentary button from pin 4 to ground using the internal pull-up. The fan turns on when the enclosure temperature rises above 30.0 C and off when it drops below 27.0 C, with PWM speed mapped from 80 at 27 C up to 255 at 45 C. Pressing the button toggles the fan manually, and the temperature is read and printed over serial at 9600 baud every 2 seconds.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A resistive rain sensor board's analog output feeds A0 (wetter = lower voltage), and the onboard LED on pin 13 lights while rain is confirmed. A DC gearmotor is driven by an H-bridge on pins 5 (close) and 6 (open), with normally-open limit switches to GND on pin 3 (closed) and pin 4 (open), and a manual open button to GND on pin 2 using the internal pull-up. The sketch must read the sensor every 20 ms and only declare rain after the reading stays below 400 for 1500 ms, clearing rain once the reading rises above 550. On confirmed rain it drives the motor closed until the closed limit switch trips or 8000 ms elapse, and the open button drives it open until the open limit switch trips or 8000 ms elapse.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: An RC receiver's channel 1 (steering) goes to D2 and channel 2 (throttle) to D3; the motor H-bridge direction pin is D5, its PWM pin is D6, and a status LED sits on D13. Each loop reads both channels with pulseIn() using a 25 ms timeout and treats a pulse as valid only if it falls between 900 and 2100 microseconds. When both channels are valid the car drives: throttle within 40 us of 1500 us stops the motor, otherwise D5 sets direction and D6 gets a PWM value mapped from 40..500 us of offset to 0..255. If no valid frame arrives for 500 ms the motor is stopped and the D13 LED blinks at 100 ms intervals until good pulses return.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A pressure switch on D2 (INPUT_PULLUP, switch closes to ground when tank pressure is below cut-in) drives a compressor contactor on D8 and a status LED on D13. When the switch has been closed and stable for 40 ms and at least 45 seconds have passed since the last stop, the relay turns on; when the switch opens and the compressor has run at least 20 seconds, the relay turns off. A 3-second start delay window is intended to ignore pressure dips at startup. The relay and LED follow the same state, active HIGH.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A 10k NTC thermistor connects from +5V to analog pin A0, with a 10k fixed resistor from A0 to ground; a momentary pushbutton ties D2 to ground using the internal pull-up, and a piezo buzzer sits on D8 to ground. The sketch samples the thermistor every 500 ms, converts the ADC reading to Celsius with the Beta equation (Beta 3950, nominal 10k at 25 C), and prints the temperature over Serial at 9600 baud. If the reading stays above 110 C for 5 continuous seconds, D8 is driven HIGH to sound the alarm; pressing the button silences it, and it re-arms only after the temperature drops below 107 C. Brief spikes above 110 C shorter than 5 seconds are ignored.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A 5V relay module signal input connects to Arduino pin 8, a momentary pushbutton from pin 2 to GND (internal pull-up enabled), and the onboard LED on pin 13 mirrors the fan. Pressing the button turns the relay and LED on and starts a 120000 ms (2 minute) countdown; pressing again while running restarts the full 2 minutes from that press. When the countdown expires the relay and LED turn off, and button presses are debounced with a 30 ms window.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: Wire a red LED from Arduino pin 8 through a 220 ohm resistor to ground, a green LED from pin 9 through a 220 ohm resistor to ground, and a momentary pushbutton from pin 2 to ground (internal pull-up enabled). Each short press of the button advances the cue light through three states in order: both LEDs off, red on (standby), green on (go), then back to both off. Presses shorter than 50 ms of bounce are ignored, and holding the button down does not keep advancing the state. The sketch also prints the current state number (0, 1, or 2) to Serial at 9600 baud for debugging.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A PIR motion sensor output feeds Arduino pin 2, a momentary reset button connects pin 3 to ground (internal pull-up enabled), and the onboard LED on pin 13 indicates a detected step. Each rising motion event increments a step counter and writes it to EEPROM address 0, but only after at least 1200 ms since the last counted step, and the sensor must return low before another step can count. Holding the button low for more than 300 ms resets the count to zero and saves it, and the current count is printed over Serial at 9600 baud on boot and after each event.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A pushbutton connects pin 2 to ground (internal pull-up enabled), a red LED with a 220-ohm resistor sits on pin 13, and a passive buzzer is on pin 8. Pressing the button starts a 180000 ms (3 minute) steep: the LED lights and stays on, and pressing the button again cancels it. When the full 3 minutes elapse the LED turns off and the buzzer beeps three 1000 Hz tones of 200 ms each, separated by 200 ms gaps, and status text is printed to Serial at 9600 baud.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A magnetic reed switch connects between Arduino pin 2 and GND (internal pullup enabled), and a piezo buzzer sits on pin 8 with the onboard LED on pin 13. After power-up the sketch waits 10 seconds before arming, then reads the reed switch: a HIGH reading means the magnet has separated and the zipper is open. Once triggered, it sounds a 2000 Hz tone on the buzzer for 200 ms, pauses 300 ms, and repeats forever while blinking the LED in sync. It never disarms until reset.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A0 reads a 0-5V current-sense signal from the saw motor; D9 drives the pump MOSFET gate and D13 mirrors it. When the ADC reading exceeds 120 the pump turns on immediately, and it stays on until the reading falls below 60 and 4000 ms have passed since the last reading above 120. The loop samples every 20 ms and prints pump state changes over Serial at 9600 baud.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A normally-closed reed switch on the tool crib door connects D2 to ground and uses the internal pull-up, so each opening or closing produces one falling edge. D13 drives an indicator LED and D9 drives a piezo buzzer; serial output runs at 9600 baud. The sketch debounces edges at 40 ms, counts every edge, treats odd counts as door-open, lights the LED and beeps 1800 Hz for 60 ms on each open, and prints edge and open counts. While the door stays open it re-beeps at 1200 Hz every 1500 ms.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: A reflective optical sensor (or reed switch) on a turntable platter is wired to digital pin 2 with INPUT_PULLUP, and it pulls the pin low twice per revolution (two marks). The onboard LED on pin 13 lights when the measured speed is within 1 RPM of 33 RPM. Every 3 seconds the sketch counts falling-edge interrupts, converts pulses to RPM (pulses/2 revolutions per 3 s, scaled by 60000/3000), and prints 'rpm=', instantaneous RPM from the last pulse period, and 'target=33' over serial at 9600 baud, followed by ' OK' or ' OFF'. If no report has happened for 10 seconds the LED is forced off.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: Wire a relay module signal input to Arduino pin 7, its coil powered from a separate 5V supply with a flyback diode, and the heater element in series with the relay's normally-open contacts on mains voltage (only if you know what you're doing). Connect an analog temperature sensor output to A0, with the sensor calibrated so that about 200 C reads as roughly 620 on the ADC. The sketch reads A0 every 250 ms and turns the relay on when the reading falls below 605, off when it rises above 635, and leaves the relay unchanged in between, so the heater holds near 200 C without relay chatter. The onboard LED on pin 13 mirrors the relay state, and the sketch prints sensor, setpoint, and heater state over Serial at 9600 baud.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: Wire a two-probe water sensor between 5V and A0 (a 10k pull-down resistor from A0 to GND keeps dry readings near 0), an active buzzer from pin 8 to GND, and a red LED with a 220 ohm resistor from pin 9 to GND. The sketch reads A0 every 50 ms and treats a reading above 300 as water; it must stay above 300 continuously for 2000 ms before alarming, so brief splashes are ignored. Once alarmed, the LED stays on and the buzzer beeps at 1 Hz (500 ms on, 500 ms off) until the reading drops back to 300 or below, which clears the alarm immediately.

style: a hobbyist with short comments
spec: A DHT22 data pin goes to D2 with 10k pull-up to 5V, a relay module signal to D7 (active HIGH, drives the compressor), the onboard LED on D13, and a 16x2 LCD in 4-bit mode wired RS=D12, E=D11, D4=D5, D5=D4, D6=D3, D7=D6. The sketch reads temperature and humidity every 2.5 seconds and turns the compressor on when temperature rises above 14.0 C, turning it off once temperature falls below 12.0 C. After any compressor shutdown it waits at least 180 seconds before allowing the relay on again. The LCD shows temperature to one decimal in Celsius on line 1 and humidity plus COOL/IDLE state on line 2.

style: a terse embedded developer with almost no comments
spec: The relay module signal input is on D8 (active HIGH), a momentary pushbutton to ground is on D2 using the internal pull-up, the onboard LED is on D13, and a current-sense analog signal from the tool's outlet is on A0. A short press of the button toggles the collector on, but it will not turn off within 2 seconds of starting; while running, any A0 reading above 120 counts as the tool being active and keeps the collector alive. If the tool has been idle (A0 at or below 120) for 30 seconds, the collector shuts itself off automatically. The relay and LED follow the same on/off state, and the button is debounced for 30 ms.

style: a beginner with chatty comments explaining each step, including what to ignore and why
spec: An Arduino Uno drives a relay module on pin 7 (active LOW, so LOW energizes the pump) that switches a 12 V wort-chiller pump. A float switch wired from pin 2 to ground (internal pull-up) reads LOW when the kettle is empty, and a momentary start/stop button from pin 3 to ground toggles operation. When running, the pump cycles ON for 5000 ms then OFF for 3000 ms, repeating, and it stops immediately if the float switch goes LOW or the button is pressed again. Serial output at 9600 baud reports start/stop state for debugging.

style: a tidy engineer who names constants and explains the design in a header comment
spec: A push button connects Arduino pin D2 to ground (internal pull-up enabled), and the on-board LED on D13 is the status indicator. A short press starts an 8-hour (28,800,000 ms) incubation: the LED blinks at 1 Hz (500 ms on, 500 ms off). When the full 8 hours elapse the LED goes solid HIGH to signal the yogurt is ready, and pressing the button again cancels or resets the timer back to idle (LED off). Button presses are debounced with a 50 ms window.
